title: April 22–25 – Korean War: In the Battle of Kapyong, the Canadians hold off the Chinese.
text: The Korean War was an armed conflict fought on the Korean Peninsula between North Korea (Democratic People's Republic of Korea; DPRK) and South Korea (Republic of Korea; ROK) and their allies. North Korea was supported by China and the Soviet Union, while South Korea was supported by the United Nations led by the United States under the auspices of the United Nations Command (UNC).

title: The Massey Report into Canadian culture is released
text: The Royal Commission on National Development in the Arts, Letters and Sciences, otherwise known as the Massey Commission, chaired by Vincent Massey, was founded in 1949 to examine Canada's cultural needs. Massey had long believed that Canadians' rich cultural history was deeply embedded in European culture but was too little known to the world.
wiki: Royal Commission on National Development in the Arts, Letters and Sciences

title: Charlotte Whitton becomes mayor of Ottawa and Canada's first woman mayor of a major city.
text: Charlotte Elizabeth Whitton was a Canadian feminist and mayor of Ottawa. She was the first woman mayor of a major city in Canada, serving from 1951 to 1956 and again from 1960 to 1964.

title: The cobalt bomb cancer therapy is first tested in London, Ontario
text: Radiation therapy or radiotherapy is a treatment using ionizing radiation, generally provided as part of cancer therapy to either kill or control the growth of malignant cells. It is normally delivered by a linear particle accelerator.

title: The Duke of Edinburgh, and The Princess Elizabeth, Duchess of Edinburgh (later Queen Elizabeth II), attend an Edmonton Eskimos home game. In the western semi-final, Edmonton beat Winnipeg 4–1
text: Prince Philip, Duke of Edinburgh, was the husband of Queen Elizabeth II and served as consort of the British monarch from her accession on 6 February 1952 until his death in 2021, making him the longest-serving royal consort in British history. Philip was born in Greece into the Greek and Danish royal families.

title: 1951 Ontario general election: Leslie Frost's PCs win a third consecutive majority
text: Leslie Miscampbell Frost was a politician in Ontario, Canada, who served as the province's 16th premier from May 4, 1949, to November 8, 1961. Due to his lengthy tenure, he gained the nickname "Old Man Ontario"; he was also known as "the Silver Fox".

title: The St. Lawrence Seaway Authority is established.
text: The St. Lawrence Seaway Management Corporation, formerly known as the St.

title: The Indian Act of Canada is revised to limit coverage of Aboriginal people, excluding Aboriginal women who married non-Aboriginal men.
text: The Indian Act is a Canadian Act of Parliament that concerns registered Indians, their bands, and the system of Indian reserves. First passed in 1876 and still in force with amendments, it is the primary document that defines how the Government of Canada interacts with the 614 First Nation bands in Canada and their members.

title: Louis St. Laurent moves into 24 Sussex Drive, the new official residence of the Prime Minister
text: Louis Stephen St. Laurent was a Canadian lawyer and politician who served as the 12th prime minister of Canada from 1948 to 1957.

title: Labatt Blue is introduced
text: Labatt Brewing Company Limited is a Canadian brewery headquartered in Toronto, Ontario. Founded in 1847, Labatt is the largest brewer in Canada.

title: The Wartime Prices and Trade Board is abolished.
text: The Wartime Prices and Trade Board is a former Canadian government agency, established on September 3, 1939, by the Mackenzie King government, under the authority of the War Measures Act, in the Department of Labour responsible for price controls and inflation control.

title: Thérèse Casgrain, the first woman to lead a provincial political party in Canada, becomes leader of the Quebec CCF.
text: Marie Thérèse Casgrain was a Canadian feminist, reformer, politician and senator. She was a leader in the fight for women's right to vote in the province of Quebec, as well as the first woman to lead a political party in Canada.

title: The Toronto Maple Leafs win their ninth Stanley Cup by defeating the Montreal Canadiens 4 games to 1. The deciding Game 5 was played at Maple Leaf Gardens in Toronto
text: The Stanley Cup is the championship trophy awarded annually to the National Hockey League (NHL) playoff champion. It is the oldest existing trophy to be awarded to a professional sports franchise in North America, and the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) considers it to be one of the "most important championships available to the sport".

title: The Ontario Hockey Association's Barrie Flyers win their first Memorial Cup by defeating the Manitoba Junior Hockey League's Winnipeg Monarchs 4 game to 0. All games were played at Shea's Amphitheatre in Winnipeg
text: The Ontario Hockey League) is one of the three major junior ice hockey leagues which constitute the Canadian Hockey League, alongside the Western Hockey League and the Quebec Maritimes Junior Hockey League. The league is for players aged 16–20.

title: The Ottawa Rough Riders win their fourth Grey Cup by defeating the Saskatchewan Roughriders 21 to 14 in the 39th Grey Cup played at Varsity Stadium in Toronto
text: The Grey Cup is both the championship game of the Canadian Football League (CFL) and the trophy awarded to the victorious team playing in the namesake championship of professional Canadian football. The game is contested between the winners of the CFL's East and West divisional playoffs and is one of Canadian television's largest annual sporting events.

title: The National Ballet of Canada gives its first performance in Eaton Auditorium, Toronto.
text: The Carlu is an historic event space in Toronto, Ontario, Canada. Opened in 1930 and known as the eponymous "Eaton's Seventh Floor", the venue was restored and reopened in 2003, renamed for its original architect.

title: Morley Callaghan – The Loved and the Lost
text: Edward Morley Callaghan was a Canadian novelist, short story writer, playwright, and TV and radio personality.

title: Harold Innis – The Bias of Communication
text: Harold Adams Innis was a Canadian professor of political economy at the University of Toronto and the author of seminal works on media, communication theory, and Canadian economic history. He helped develop the staples thesis, which holds that Canada's culture, political history, and economy have been decisively influenced by the exploitation and export of a series of "staples" such as fur, fish, lumber, wheat, mi…

title: See 1951 Governor General's Awards for a complete list of winners and finalists for those awards.
text: The 15th Governor General's Awards for Literary Merit were presented on June 13, 1952 for works of Canadian literature published in 1951. The awards in this period had no monetary prize and were just an honour for the authors.

title: Stephen Leacock Award: Eric Nicol, The Roving I
text: The Stephen Leacock Memorial Medal for Humour, also known as the Stephen Leacock Medal for Humour or just the Leacock Medal, is an annual Canadian literary award presented for the best book of humour written in English by a Canadian writer, published or self-published in the previous year. The silver medal, designed by sculptor Emanuel Hahn, is a tribute to well-known Canadian humorist Stephen Leacock and is accom…
wiki: Stephen Leacock Memorial Medal for Humour

title: “Too Young” by Nat King Cole with Les Baxter
text: "Too Young" is a popular song, with music written by Sidney Lippman and lyrics by Sylvia Dee. A recording of the song was released by Nat King Cole in 1951, which reached No.
wiki: Too Young (Sidney Lippman and Sylvia Dee song)
listen: Too Young Nat King Cole with Les Baxter

title: “Because of You” by Tony Bennett with Percy Faith
text: "Because of You" is a popular song written by Arthur Hammerstein and Dudley Wilkinson in 1940. It was first recorded by Larry Clinton and His Orchestra on December 12, 1940, and was released March 28, 1941 on Bluebird 11094.
listen: Because of You Tony Bennett with Percy Faith

title: “How High the Moon” by Les Paul and Mary Ford
text: "How High the Moon" is a jazz standard with lyrics by Nancy Hamilton and music by Morgan Lewis. It was first featured in the 1940 Broadway revue Two for the Show, where it was sung by Alfred Drake and Frances Comstock.
listen: How High the Moon Les Paul and Mary Ford

title: “Come On-a My House” by Rosemary Clooney
text: "Come On-a My House" is a song written by Ross Bagdasarian and William Saroyan and originally released by Rosemary Clooney in 1951. Bagdasarian and Saroyan were cousins who wrote the song while driving across New Mexico in the summer of 1939.
listen: Come On-a My House Rosemary Clooney

title: “Be My Love” by Mario Lanza with Ray Sinatra and Jeff Alexander
text: "Be My Love" is a song with lyrics by Sammy Cahn and music by Nicholas Brodszky. Published in 1950, it was written for Mario Lanza, who sang it with Kathryn Grayson in the 1950 movie The Toast of New Orleans.
listen: Be My Love Mario Lanza with Ray Sinatra and Jeff Alexander

title: “On Top of Old Smoky” by The Weavers and Terry Gilkyson with Vic Schoen
text: "On Top of Old Smoky" is a traditional folk song and nursery rhyme of the United States. It is catalogued as Roud Folk Song Index No.
listen: On Top of Old Smoky The Weavers and Terry Gilkyson with Vic Schoen

title: “Cold, Cold Heart” by Tony Bennett with Percy Faith
text: "Cold, Cold Heart" is a country music and pop song written and first recorded by Hank Williams. This blues ballad is both a classic of honky-tonk and an entry in the Great American Songbook.
listen: Cold, Cold Heart Tony Bennett with Percy Faith

title: “If” by Perry Como with Mitchell Ayres
text: "If" is a popular song with music written by Tolchard Evans and the lyrics written by Robert Hargreaves and Stanley J. Damerell. The song was written in 1934, but the most popular versions were recorded in 1950–1951.
listen: If Perry Como with Mitchell Ayres

title: “The Loveliest Night of the Year” by Mario Lanza
text: "The Loveliest Night of the Year" is a popular song. The music was first published as a waltz called "Sobre las olas" in 1888, written by Juventino P. Rosas.
wiki: The Loveliest Night of the Year
listen: The Loveliest Night of the Year Mario Lanza

title: “Tennessee Waltz” by Patti Page
text: "Tennessee Waltz" is an American popular country music song with lyrics by Redd Stewart and music by Pee Wee King written in 1946 and first released in January 1948. The song became a multimillion seller via a 1950 recording – as "The Tennessee Waltz" – by Patti Page.
listen: Tennessee Waltz Patti Page

title: “Jezebel” by Frankie Laine with The Norman Luboff Choir and Mitch Miller
text: "Jezebel" is a 1951 popular song written by American songwriter Wayne Shanklin. It was recorded by Frankie Laine with the Norman Luboff Choir and Mitch Miller and his orchestra on April 4, 1951 and released by Columbia Records as catalog number 39367.
listen: Jezebel Frankie Laine with The Norman Luboff Choir and Mitch Miller

title: “I Get Ideas” by Tony Martin with Henri René
text: "I Get Ideas" is a popular song which has been recorded by various musicians and used in a number of films and television episodes.
listen: I Get Ideas Tony Martin with Henri René

title: “Mockin' Bird Hill” by Les Paul and Mary Ford
text: "Mockin' Bird Hill" is a song written in 3⁄4 time by Calle Jularbo, with lyrics by George Vaughn Horton. It is perhaps best known through recordings by Patti Page, Horton's own Pinetoppers, and the duo of Les Paul and Mary Ford in 1951, or by Donna Fargo's 1977 version, but many other artists have also recorded the song.
listen: Mockin' Bird Hill Les Paul and Mary Ford

title: “My Heart Cries for You” by Guy Mitchell & Mitch Miller
text: "My Heart Cries for You" is a popular song, adapted by Carl Sigman and Percy Faith from an 18th-century French melody. The song has been recorded by many singers, the most successful of which was recorded by Guy Mitchell.
listen: My Heart Cries for You Guy Mitchell & Mitch Miller

title: “(It's No) Sin” by Eddy Howard
text: " Sin" is a popular song with music by George Hoven and lyrics by Chester R. Shull. It was a No.
listen: (It's No) Sin Eddy Howard

title: “Sound Off” by Vaughn Monroe
text: Vaughn Wilton Monroe was an American baritone singer, trumpeter and big band leader who was most popular in the 1940s and 1950s. He has two stars on the Hollywood Walk of Fame, one for recording and another for radio performance.
listen: Sound Off Vaughn Monroe

title: “Sweet Violets” by Dinah Shore with Henri René
text: "Sweet Violets" is an American song that contains classic example of a "censored rhyme", where the expected rhyme of each couplet or verse is replaced with a surprising word which segues into the next couplet or chorus. For example, the first couplets of the version recorded by Dinah Shore are: There once was a farmer who took a young miss In back of the barn where he gave her a...
listen: Sweet Violets Dinah Shore with Henri René

title: “The World Is Waiting for the Sunrise” by Les Paul and Mary Ford
text: "The World Is Waiting for the Sunrise" is a post-World War I popular song with lyrics by Canadian-born American actor Eugene Lockhart, and music composed by Canadian-born concert pianist Ernest Seitz in 1918. He later claimed he conceived the refrain when he was 12 years old.
wiki: The World Is Waiting for the Sunrise
listen: The World Is Waiting for the Sunrise Les Paul and Mary Ford

title: “My Truly, Truly Fair” by Guy Mitchell & Mitch Miller
text: "My Truly, Truly Fair" is a popular song written by Bob Merrill. It was published in 1951.
listen: My Truly, Truly Fair Guy Mitchell & Mitch Miller

title: “Aba Daba Honeymoon” by Debbie Reynolds & Carleton Carpenter with Georgie Stoll
text: "Aba Daba Honeymoon" is a show tune with lyrics by Arthur Fields and music by Walter Donovan. It was published in 1914 by Leo Feist.
listen: Aba Daba Honeymoon Debbie Reynolds & Carleton Carpenter with Georgie Stoll

title: “Rose, Rose, I Love You” by Frankie Laine and The Norman Luboff Choir with Paul Weston
text: "Rose, Rose, I Love You" is a 1940 Mandarin popular song composed by Chen Gexin and first recorded by Yao Lee. An English-language version whose lyrics have little in common with the original Mandarin was first recorded by Frankie Laine in 1951.
listen: Rose, Rose, I Love You Frankie Laine and The Norman Luboff Choir with Paul Weston

title: “Down Yonder” by Del Wood
text: Down Yonder is a popular American song with music and lyrics by L. Wolfe Gilbert. It was first published in 1921, and was introduced in the same year at the Orpheum Theater, New Orleans.
listen: Down Yonder Del Wood

title: “I Apologize” by Billy Eckstine
text: "I Apologize" is a popular song written by Al Hoffman, Al Goodhart, and Ed Nelson.
listen: I Apologize Billy Eckstine

title: “Would I Love You (Love You, Love You)” by Patti Page
text: "Would I Love You" is a pop song composed by Harold Spina with lyrics by Bob Russell. It was published in 1950 and covered by many different musicians.
wiki: Would I Love You (Love You, Love You)
listen: Would I Love You (Love You, Love You) Patti Page

title: “You're Just in Love” by Perry Como & The Fontane Sisters with Mitchell Ayres
text: "You're Just in Love" is a popular song by Irving Berlin. It was published in 1950 and was first performed by Ethel Merman and Russell Nype in Call Me Madam, a musical comedy that made its debut at the Imperial Theatre in New York City on October 12 that year.
listen: You're Just in Love Perry Como & The Fontane Sisters with Mitchell Ayres

title: “Undecided” by Ames Brothers with The Les Brown Orchestra
text: "Undecided" is a popular song written by Sid Robin with music by Charlie Shavers and published in 1938.
listen: Undecided Ames Brothers with The Les Brown Orchestra

title: “The Thing” by Phil Harris with Walter Scharf
text: "The Thing" is a novelty song by Charles Randolph Grean released in 1950. The song received heavy airplay, spending 14 weeks on the Billboard charts.
listen: The Thing Phil Harris with Walter Scharf

title: The Government of the United Kingdom announces abandonment of the Tanganyika groundnut scheme for the cultivation of peanuts in the Tanganyika Territory, with the writing off of £36.5M debt.
text: The Tanganyika groundnut scheme, or East Africa groundnut scheme, was a failed attempt by the British government to cultivate tracts of its African trust territory Tanganyika with peanuts. Launched in the aftermath of World War II in 1946 by the Labour Party administration of prime minister Clement Attlee, the goal was to produce urgently needed oilseeds on a projected 3 million acres (5,000 sq miles, or over 12,0…

title: In a criminal court in West Germany, Ilse Koch, The "Witch of Buchenwald", wife of the commandant of the Buchenwald concentration camp, is sentenced to life imprisonment.
text: Margarete Ilse Koch was a German war criminal who committed atrocities while her husband Karl-Otto Koch was the commandant at Buchenwald. Though Ilse Koch had no official position in Nazi Germany, she became one of the most infamous Nazi figures at the war's end and was referred to as the "Kommandeuse of Buchenwald".

title: Winter of Terror: Avalanches in the Alps kill 240 and bury 45,000 for a time, in Switzerland, Austria and Italy.
text: The Winter of Terror was a three-month period during the winter of 1950–1951 during which an unprecedented number of avalanches took place in the Alps in Switzerland, Austria and Italy. The series of 649 avalanches killed over 265 people and caused large amounts of damage to residential and other human-made structures.

title: Mount Lamington in Papua New Guinea erupts catastrophically, killing nearly 3,000 people and causing great devastation in Oro Province.
text: Mount Lamington is an andesitic stratovolcano in the Oro Province of Papua New Guinea. The forested peak of the volcano had not been recognised as such until its devastating eruption in 1951 that caused about 3,000 deaths.

title: Dutch author Anne de Vries releases the first volume of his children's novel Journey Through the Night (Reis door de nacht), set during World War II.
text: Anne de Vries was a Dutch teacher and writer, particularly famous in the Netherlands for his novels of regional life. Born in the village of Kloosterveen near Assen, de Vries married Alida Gerdina van Wermeskerken in 1930 and the couple had five children.

title: The Convention People's Party wins national elections in Gold Coast (British colony).
text: General elections were held in Gold Coast on 8 February 1951. Although elections had been held for the Legislative Council since 1925, the Council did not have complete control over the legislation, and the voting franchise was limited to residents of urban areas meeting property requirements and the councils of chiefs.

title: February 1–2 – The 1951 Nepalese revolution leads to agreement for a democratic constitution.
text: The 1950–1951 Nepalese revolution, also known as Saat Saalko Kranti was a revolution in the Kingdom of Nepal that brought an end to Rana rule of Nepal which had lasted for 104 years.

title: The United Nations General Assembly declares that China is an aggressor in the Korean War, in United Nations General Assembly Resolution 498.
text: The United Nations General Assembly is one of the six principal organs of the United Nations (UN), serving as its main deliberative, policymaking, and representative organ. Currently in its 81st session, its powers, composition, functions, and procedures are set out in Chapter IV of the United Nations Charter.

title: Woodbridge train wreck: A Pennsylvania Railroad passenger train derails near Woodbridge Township, New Jersey, killing 85 people and injuring over 500, in one of the worst rail disasters in American history.
text: On February 6, 1951, a Pennsylvania Railroad train derailed on a temporary wooden trestle in Woodbridge, New Jersey, United States, killing 85 passengers. It remains New Jersey's deadliest train wreck, the deadliest U.S. derailment since 1918 and the deadliest peacetime rail disaster in U.S. history.

title: The seven-nation Commonwealth Consultative Committee meets to discuss the Colombo Plan for south and south-east Asia.
text: The Colombo plan is a regional intergovernmental organization that began operations on 1 July 1951. The organization was conceived at an international conference, The Commonwealth Conference on Foreign Affairs held in Colombo, Ceylon in January 1950, and was attended by the finance ministers of Australia, the United Kingdom, Canada, Ceylon, Pakistan and New Zealand, and the prime ministers of Ceylon and India.

title: Muhammad Reza Shah marries Soraya Esfandiary-Bakhtiari.
text: Mohammad Reza Pahlavi was the last Shah of Iran, reigning from 1941 to 1979 as the second monarch of the Pahlavi dynasty. He succeeded his father, Reza Shah, and ruled the Imperial State of Iran until his overthrow in the Islamic Revolution, which abolished the nearly 2,500-year-old Iranian monarchy.

title: Jean Lee becomes the last woman hanged in Australia, when she and her two pimps are hanged for the murder and torture of a 73-year-old bookmaker.
text: Jean Lee was an Australian murderer who, together with her lover Robert Clayton and accomplice Norman Andrews, was convicted for the 1949 killing of William 'Pop' Kent, an SP bookmaker from the Melbourne suburb of Carlton. The victim was bound to a chair, tortured with the aim of finding hidden money, and finally strangled.

title: The first Pan American Games open in Buenos Aires.
text: The Pan American Games, known as the Pan Am Games, is a continental multi-sport event in the Americas first held in 1951. It features thousands of athletes participating in competitions to win different summer sports.

title: The Twenty-second Amendment to the United States Constitution, limiting Presidents to two terms, is ratified.
text: The Twenty-second Amendment to the United States Constitution limits the number of times a person may be elected to the office of President of the United States to two, and sets additional eligibility conditions for presidents who succeed to the unexpired terms of their predecessors. Congress approved the Twenty-second Amendment on March 21, 1947, and submitted it to the state legislatures for ratification.
wiki: Twenty-second Amendment to the United States Constitution

title: The trial of Julius and Ethel Rosenberg for conspiracy to commit espionage begins in the United States.
text: Julius Rosenberg and Ethel Rosenberg (née Greenglass; September 28, 1915 – June 19, 1953) were an American married couple who were convicted of spying for the Soviet Union, including providing top-secret information about American radar, sonar, jet propulsion engines, and nuclear weapon designs. They were executed by the federal government of the United States in 1953 using New York's state execution chamber in Si…

title: West Germany joins UNESCO.
text: The United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization is a specialized agency of the United Nations (UN) with the aim of promoting world peace and security through international cooperation in education, arts, sciences and culture. It has 194 member states and 12 associate members, as well as partners in the non-governmental, intergovernmental and private sector.

title: Second Red Scare: In the United States, Julius and Ethel Rosenberg are convicted of conspiracy to commit espionage. On April 5 they are sentenced to death.
text: McCarthyism is a political practice defined by the accusation and investigation of left-wing individuals of communist and Soviet influence on American institutions and of Soviet espionage in the United States during the late 1940s through the 1950s, heavily associated with the McCarthy era. After the mid-1950s, U.S. senator Joseph McCarthy, who had spearheaded the campaign, gradually lost his public popularity aft…

title: Rodgers and Hammerstein's The King and I opens on Broadway, and runs for three years. It is the first of their musicals specifically written for an actress (Gertrude Lawrence). Lawrence is stricken with cancer during the run of the show,…
text: Rodgers and Hammerstein was a theater-writing team of composer Richard Rodgers and lyricist-dramatist Oscar Hammerstein II (1895–1960), who together created a series of innovative and influential American musicals. Their musical theater writing partnership has been called the greatest of the 20th century.

title: The 23rd Academy Awards Ceremony is held; All About Eve wins the Best Picture award and five others.
text: All About Eve is a 1950 American drama film written and directed by Joseph L. Mankiewicz, and produced by Darryl F. Zanuck. It is based on the 1946 short story "The Wisdom of Eve" by Mary Orr, although Orr does not receive a screen credit.

title: Remington Rand delivers the first UNIVAC I computer to the United States Census Bureau.
text: Remington Rand, Inc., was an early American business machine manufacturer, originally a typewriter manufacturer and in a later incarnation the manufacturer of the UNIVAC line of mainframe computers. Formed in 1927 following a merger, Remington Rand was a diversified conglomerate making other office equipment, electric shavers, etc.

title: Soviet space dogs Dezik and Tsygan become the first to enter space, in a 15-minute sub-orbital spaceflight from Kapustin Yar in an R-1 rocket, being safely parachuted back to earth.
text: In the 1950s and 1960s, the Soviet space program used dogs for suborbital and orbital space flights as proof-of-concept to determine whether human spaceflight was feasible. The Soviet space program typically used female dogs due to their anatomical compatibility with the spacesuit.

title: Janie Moore, C. S. Lewis' so-called adoptive mother, dies.
text: Clive Staples Lewis was a British author, literary scholar and Anglican lay theologian. He held academic positions in English literature at both Magdalen College, Oxford (1925–1954), and Magdalene College, Cambridge (1954–1963).

title: The American writer Flannery O'Connor leaves hospital after being diagnosed with lupus at the age of 25.
text: Mary Flannery O'Connor was an American novelist, short story writer, and essayist. She wrote two novels and 31 short stories, as well as a number of reviews and commentaries.

title: Hank Ketcham's American comic strip Dennis the Menace first appears in 16 American newspapers. The strip is originally distributed by the Post-Hall Syndicate.
text: Henry King Ketcham was an American cartoonist who created the Dennis the Menace comic strip, writing and drawing it from 1951 to 1994, when he retired from drawing the daily cartoon and took up painting full-time in his home studio. In 1953, he received the Reuben Award for the strip, which continues today in the hands of other cartoonists.

title: The homonymous British comic strip Dennis the Menace first appears in the Scottish anthology comic magazine The Beano, in issue 452 (dated March 17, 1951), on sale from March 12. It is the longest-running strip in the comic. The idea and…
text: Music hall is a type of British theatrical entertainment that was most popular from the early Victorian era until around World War I. It faded away after 1918 as the halls rebranded their entertainment as variety. Perceptions of a distinction in Britain between bold and scandalous music hall entertainment and subsequent, more respectable variety entertainment differ.

title: Spring – Arthur C. Clarke's short story "The Sentinel", which will form a basis for the film 2001: A Space Odyssey (1968) and a subsequent novel, is published as "Sentinel of Eternity" in the only issue ever produced of the American…
text: Sir Arthur Charles Clarke was an English science fiction writer, inventor, undersea explorer and TV series host. He popularised space travel and wrote many books and many essays for popular magazines.

title: Joe Orton enters the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art in London, where he meets his lover and ultimate murderer Kenneth Halliwell.
text: The Royal Academy of Dramatic Art is a drama school in London, England, which provides vocational conservatoire training for theatre, film, television, and radio. It is based in Bloomsbury, Central London, close to the Senate House complex of the University of London, and is a founding member of the Federation of Drama Schools.

title: Frank Hardy is acquitted of criminal libel in the Australian state of Victoria over his self-published 1950 roman à clef on corruption in Melbourne political life, Power Without Glory.
text: Francis Joseph Hardy, published as Frank J. Hardy and also under the pseudonym Ross Franklyn, was an Australian novelist and writer. He is best known for his 1950 novel Power Without Glory, and for his later political activism.

title: J. D. Salinger's coming-of-age story The Catcher in the Rye is published by Little, Brown and Company in New York City.
text: Jerome David Salinger was an American writer best known for his 1951 novel The Catcher in the Rye. Salinger published several short stories in Story magazine in 1940, before serving in World War II. In 1948, his critically acclaimed story "A Perfect Day for Bananafish" appeared in The New Yorker, which published much of his later work.

title: The Peggy Guggenheim Collection at the Palazzo Venier dei Leoni in Venice is first opened to the public.
text: The Peggy Guggenheim Collection is an art museum on the Grand Canal in the Dorsoduro sestiere of Venice, Italy. It is one of the most visited attractions in Venice.

title: Festival Star emblem by Abram Games.
text: The Festival Star was the graphic symbol designed by Abram Games for the 1951 Festival of Britain. Games was one of 12 artists invited to submit designs to the Arts Council and the Council of Industrial Design in 1948, and won the limited competition.

title: Royal Festival Hall by Leslie Martin, Peter Moro and Robert Matthew.
text: Sir John Leslie Martin was an English architect, and a leading advocate of the International Style. Martin's most famous building is the Royal Festival Hall.

title: Dome of Discovery by Ralph Tubbs.
text: The Dome of Discovery was a temporary exhibition building designed by architect Ralph Tubbs for the Festival of Britain celebrations which took place on London's South Bank in 1951, alongside the River Thames. The consulting engineers were Freeman Fox & Partners, in particular Oleg Kerensky and Gilbert Roberts.

title: Skylon by Philip Powell, Hidalgo Moya and Felix Samuely.
text: The Skylon was a futuristic-looking, slender, vertical, cigar-shaped steel tensegrity structure located by the Thames in London, that gave the illusion of floating above the ground, built in 1951 for the Festival of Britain. A popular joke of the period was that, like the British economy of 1951, "It had no visible means of support".
